blocks.text: A test rig measures only the angle of a motor shaft. A student asks the obvious question: can the speed be recovered from that single signal? Differentiating the angle gives a noisy answer, but a more fundamental question comes first: does the angle record contain enough information to reconstruct the whole state at all? Observability answers it before any sensor is bought.

blocks.markdown: A linear system $\dot x=Ax+Bu$, $y=Cx$ is **observable** if the initial state $x(0)$ can be determined uniquely from the measured output $y(t)$ and the known input $u(t)$ over a finite time interval. Because the input and the system model are known, the effect of $u$ can be subtracted, so observability depends only on the pair $(A,C)$, not on $B$.

blocks.title: Observability matrix
blocks.text: For $A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ and $C\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times n}$, the observability matrix stacks the output matrix and its successive products with $A$: $\mathcal{O}=[C;\,CA;\,CA^2;\,\dots;\,CA^{n-1}]$ ($np\times n$). The pair $(A,C)$ is observable if and only if $\operatorname{rank}\mathcal{O}=n$.

blocks.markdown: The idea: $y=Cx$ shows one linear combination of the state; $\dot y=CAx+CBu$ shows another; each further derivative reveals one more combination $CA^kx$. If the $n$ rows are independent, the derivatives of $y$ determine $x$. If they are dependent, some combination of states never shows up in $y$ however long we watch: an *unobservable mode*.

blocks.title: Which sensor on a spring-mass plant?
blocks.prompt: A mass-spring-damper has states $x_1$ (position) and $x_2$ (velocity) with $A=\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\-4&-1\end{bmatrix}$ (so $k/m=4$, $c/m=1$). Test observability for (a) a position sensor, $C=[1\;\;0]$ and (b) a velocity sensor, $C=[0\;\;1]$.

steps.text: Position sensor: $CA=[1\;0]A=[0\;1]$, so the stacked matrix is the identity.

Both determinants are nonzero, so both sensors make the plant observable. With a spring ($k>0$) the position feeds back into the acceleration, so the velocity record also carries position information.

blocks.answer: Observable with either sensor; the position sensor is the simplest case ($\mathcal{O}=I$).

rows: Some mode cannot be moved by the input
Some mode is invisible in the output
State feedback cannot place that pole
An observer cannot estimate that state
blocks.caption: Controllability and observability side by side (dual concepts).

blocks.title: Duality
blocks.text: The pair $(A,C)$ is observable if and only if the pair $(A^T,C^T)$ is controllable, because $\mathcal{O}(A,C)=\mathcal{C}(A^T,C^T)^T$. Every theorem about controllability therefore has a mirror theorem about observability: state feedback and the observer gain are dual design problems.

blocks.title: Duality in practice
blocks.prompt: For $A=\begin{bmatrix}-2&1\\0&-5\end{bmatrix}$ and $C=[0\;\;1]$, test observability directly and by checking controllability of the dual pair $(A^T,C^T)$.

steps.text: The two tests agree: the pair is not observable. Physically $\dot x_2=-5x_2$ evolves on its own and the output is $x_2$, so the output never sees $x_1$, whose eigenvalue $-2$ is the unobservable mode.

blocks.answer: Not observable (rank 1); the unobservable mode is at $s=-2$. Both the direct and the dual test agree.

blocks.markdown: **Choosing a sensor set.** For a two-state plant you need $\operatorname{rank}\mathcal{O}=2$. Sometimes a single sensor works and sometimes it cannot, depending on how the states couple. A free inertia with viscous friction is the standard trap: nothing in the dynamics depends on position, so a velocity sensor can never reveal it.

blocks.title: A free inertia with friction
blocks.prompt: A rotating disc has states $\theta$ (angle) and $\omega$ (angular velocity), with $A=\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\0&-2\end{bmatrix}$. Compare an angle sensor with a speed sensor.

steps.text: Speed sensor $C=[0\;1]$: $CA=[0\;-2]$, which is parallel to $C$.
The speed record is a decaying exponential that does not depend on the angle, so the initial angle cannot be recovered from it.

blocks.answer: The angle sensor makes the plant observable; the speed sensor alone leaves the angle unobservable.

blocks.title: Observable on paper is not the same as well-measured
blocks.text: A pair can be observable but poorly conditioned, so that a state is recoverable only by dividing by a tiny number and amplifying noise. Check how large the rank-test determinant is relative to typical values, and prefer sensors that measure the state of interest directly.

points: The pair $(A,C)$ is observable if and only if the stacked matrix $[C;\,CA;\cdots;CA^{n-1}]$ has rank $n$.
Duality: $(A,C)$ is observable exactly when $(A^T,C^T)$ is controllable.
Whether a sensor set makes a plant observable depends on the coupling between states; a measurement of a state that nothing else depends on cannot reveal the state it does not drive.

questions.stem: For a plant with three states and one output, which stacked matrix must have rank 3 for observability?

distractorRationale.a: The output and its successive derivatives give three independent combinations of the state.
distractorRationale.b: This is the controllability matrix and involves the input matrix instead.
distractorRationale.c: These are Markov parameters of the transfer function, not the observability test.
distractorRationale.d: The powers must be of $A$, not of $C$, and $C$ is not square in general.

questions.explanation: Observability stacks $C$, $CA$, $CA^2$ so that each row is one more output derivative with respect to the unforced dynamics. The controllability matrix and the Markov parameters answer different questions.

questions.stem: If the observability matrix of a four-state system has rank 3, what is true?

options.text: The input cannot influence one combination of states
The output equals three times the input
One independent combination of states never appears in the output

questions.correctOptionText: One independent combination of states never appears in the output

distractorRationale.a: That describes an uncontrollable mode and depends on $B$.
distractorRationale.b: A four-state system has four poles regardless of observability.
distractorRationale.c: The rank test says nothing about the input-output gain.
distractorRationale.d: The rank deficiency counts the dimension of the unobservable subspace.

questions.explanation: A rank of three for $n=4$ means the output reveals three independent combinations of the state while one combination is invisible. The input matrix plays no role in this test.

questions.stem: Which statement of duality is correct?

options.text: $(A,C)$ is observable if and only if $(A,C)$ is controllable
$(A,C)$ is observable if and only if $(A^T,C^T)$ is controllable
$(A,C)$ is observable if and only if $A$ is stable
$(A,C)$ is observable if and only if $CB\neq0$

questions.correctOptionText: $(A,C)$ is observable if and only if $(A^T,C^T)$ is controllable

distractorRationale.a: Controllability involves $B$, so the same pair cannot be tested this way.
distractorRationale.b: Transposing swaps the roles of $B$ and $C$, so the tests are mirrors.
distractorRationale.d: The product $CB$ is a Markov parameter and does not decide observability.

questions.explanation: Since $\mathcal{O}(A,C)=\mathcal{C}(A^T,C^T)^T$ and a matrix and its transpose have the same rank, observability of $(A,C)$ is equivalent to controllability of $(A^T,C^T)$. This is why observer design mirrors state-feedback design.

questions.stem: A 4 kg cart on a spring of stiffness 100 N/m (no damping) has states position and velocity, so $A=\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\-25&0\end{bmatrix}$. Only a velocity sensor is fitted. Is the plant observable?

options.text: No, because the sensor does not measure position directly
No, because there is no damping
Yes, but only if the cart starts at zero velocity

distractorRationale.a: Observability does not require every state to be measured directly.
distractorRationale.b: Damping is not required for observability.
distractorRationale.c: The spring couples position into the velocity equation, so the velocity record carries position information.
distractorRationale.d: Observability holds for all initial states and is not tied to a particular one.

questions.explanation: The stacked matrix is $\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\-25&0\end{bmatrix}$ with determinant 25, so the rank is two. The spring makes acceleration depend on position, so the velocity trace oscillates with a phase and amplitude that encode the initial position.

questions.stem: True or false: the choice of the input signal $u(t)$ affects whether a linear system is observable.
questions.explanation: Observability is a property of $(A,C)$ only. The known input contributes a known term to the output that can be computed and subtracted, so it neither helps nor hinders reconstruction of the initial state.

questions.stem: For $A=\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\-8&-6\end{bmatrix}$ and $C=[3\;\;1]$, compute the determinant of the observability matrix $[C;\,CA]$ (dimensionless).
questions.explanation: Here $CA=[3\;1]A=[-8\;\;3-6]=[-8\;\;-3]$, so $\mathcal{O}=\begin{bmatrix}3&1\\-8&-3\end{bmatrix}$. The determinant is $3(-3)-1(-8)=-9+8=-1$, nonzero, so the pair is observable.

questions.stem: A plant has $A=\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\-6&-5\end{bmatrix}$ and output matrix $C=[1\;\;\gamma]$. There are two positive values of $\gamma$ (dimensionless) that make the system unobservable. Give the smaller one.
questions.explanation: With $CA=[-6\gamma\;\;1-5\gamma]$, $\det\mathcal{O}=1-5\gamma+6\gamma^2=(1-2\gamma)(1-3\gamma)$. This vanishes at $\gamma=1/3$ and $\gamma=1/2$, so the smaller value is $1/3\approx0.333$ (where $C$ is a left eigenvector of $A$ for eigenvalue $-2$).

questions.stem: A plant has $A=\begin{bmatrix}-3&2\\0&-6\end{bmatrix}$ and output $y=x_2$ (so $C=[0\;\;1]$). The plant is not observable. What is the time constant, in seconds, of the unobservable mode?
questions.explanation: Here $\dot x_2=-6x_2$ is independent of $x_1$ and the output is $x_2$, so the output shows only the mode at $-6$; $\mathcal{O}=\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\0&-6\end{bmatrix}$ has rank 1. The unobservable mode is the remaining eigenvalue $-3$, so its time constant is $1/3\approx0.333$ s.

questions.stem: State the duality between controllability and observability and explain, using it, why the observability test has the form of a stacked matrix of $C,CA,\dots,CA^{n-1}$.
markingGuide: States that $(A,C)$ is observable if and only if $(A^T,C^T)$ is controllable.
Writes the controllability matrix of the dual pair, $[C^T\;A^TC^T\cdots(A^T)^{n-1}C^T]$.
Observes that transposing it gives the stacked matrix with rows $C, CA,\dots,CA^{n-1}$.
Notes that rank is unchanged by transposition, so rank $n$ in one is rank $n$ in the other.
questions.explanation: The dual pair has controllability matrix $[C^T\;A^TC^T\cdots]$, and transposing it yields rows $C, CA,\dots,CA^{n-1}$ since $(A^T)^kC^T$ transposes to $CA^k$. A matrix and its transpose have the same rank, so the two tests are equivalent.

questions.stem: Two tanks are connected in cascade: $\dot x_1=-x_1$ (upstream level deviation, draining only into tank 2) and $\dot x_2=x_1-2x_2$. Decide which single level sensor, on tank 1 or on tank 2, makes the plant observable, and justify your answer with the rank test and a physical argument.
markingGuide: Sensor on tank 1: $C=[1\;0]$, $CA=[-1\;0]$, rank 1 so tank 2 is unobservable.
Sensor on tank 2: $C=[0\;1]$, $CA=[1\;-2]$, determinant $-1\neq0$, so rank 2 and the plant is observable.
Physical argument: flow goes only downstream, so the downstream level is affected by the upstream level but not vice versa; the downstream sensor sees both, the upstream sensor sees only itself.
questions.explanation: The upstream level evolves independently of tank 2, so a sensor there carries no information about $x_2$ and the observability matrix has rank 1. A sensor on tank 2 has $\mathcal{O}=\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\1&-2\end{bmatrix}$ with determinant $-1$, and physically the downstream level integrates the upstream signal, so it reveals both states.
